title: Sharp Regret of Learning the Neyman Allocation under Fourth-Moment Budgets

gap_reasons: The delivered characterization gives matching fixed-budget and divergent-sublinear-budget constants; sharp finite-positive budget-to-horizon ratios remain unresolved, as the framing correctly states. The unrestricted-history lemma supplies the common dominating experiment, information calculation and prior integration needed for the converse without restricting competitor propensities. The Clip-OGD comparison cannot establish novelty of logarithmic regret itself, already obtained under bounded outcomes by [ClipSMT](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.14341) and [Noarov et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.17427); the substantive advance is the exact full-law coefficient and quantitative growing-budget analysis. tldr: For every divergent sublinear fourth-moment budget, the sharp full-law price of learning the raw Horvitz--Thompson allocation is \(R_T(\beta_T)\sim(99/16)\beta_T\log(T/\beta_T)\). An explicit budget-aware original-record policy has a uniform \(O(\beta_T)\) remainder, and the converse covers every positive Borel policy and correlated exogenous seed law. Fixed budgets have coefficient \((99\beta-9)/16\), including \(981/16\) at ten; the infinite budget-to-horizon ratio has normalized value \(1/4\). Sharp finite positive ratios remain open. Theorem 4 gives a different-policy stationary-iid guarantee for the same hindsight objective used by Clip-OGD, with an explicit oracle correction.
gap: Clip-OGD supplies a design-based hindsight-regret benchmark, and ClipSMT supplies bounded-iid logarithmic-order tracking. Their stated results do not determine a sharp horizon--fourth-moment-budget frontier or its transition constants. \cite{dai2023clipogd,neopane2025logarithmic}
fill: Matching bounds uniform in \((T,\beta)\), an exact affine fixed-budget coefficient, and the uncapped \(T/4\) endpoint establish the envelope scale. The sharp transition question derives its limiting experiment rather than assuming a parametric tail shape. The common-seed information lemma keeps the full original-record decision class.
